newsitem.title: USA: US Marines stage biggest evacuation from Freetown.
newsitem.headline: US Marines stage biggest evacuation from Freetown.

text.p: U.S. Marines deploying a devastating array of firepower on Tuesday airlifted 1,220 civilians trapped by gun battles in Sierra Leone to a warship in the largest single-day non-combatant evacuation carried out by Marines and Navy.

The hangar deck of the USS Kearsarge resembled a refugee camp as waves of West Africans, Lebanese and some remaining Europeans and Americans were brought on board from CH-46 Sea Knight and CH-53 Sea Stallion helicopters.
The Marines took no chances after a day of merciless gun battles between Nigerian troops trying to reverse a coup in Freetown and rebels allied to the coup soldiers.
The deployment was an emergency operation to rescue more than 600 civilians trapped by fighting in a Freetown hotel for close to 12 hours on Monday, huddling in a stifling basement for safety.
"It's a relief to be on board. We never thouht we would get out alive from that hotel," said Lebanese businessman Hashim Bazam.

The May 25 coup, Sierra Leone's third in five years, was followed by widespread looting and violence. Rebels from the bush have flocked to Freetown to join the coup soldiers and there have been reports of killings of Lebanese businessmen and rapes of women aid workers.
"We salute you Americans," said a Sierra Leonean woman as she was helped on board one of the helicopters.
As the helicopters landed and took off in a cloud of sand, rebels of the Revolutionary United Front cruised along the beach road in looted trucks.

Some 500 Marines from the Kearsarge landed along the beach. They brought ashore light armoured vehicles and used landing craft air cushions to bring missile launching vehicles onshore equipped with optically tracked guided missiles.

Task Force spokesman Captain Jason Johnston told reporters the Marines had evacuated more than 900 people, mostly Americans and Europeans, last Friday, then another 300 foreigners on Sunday, bringing the total including Tuesday's evacuees to nearly 2,500.

Marines were called in again on Monday after the International Committee of the Red Cross brokered a truce in the fighting around the Mammy Yoko Hotel but they aborted an emergency evacuation plan because of gunfire on the ground.
"We had to stop after indications that the situation was getting a little worse," Johnston said.

Tuesday's evacuees included staff from the British High Commission, the latest diplomatic mission to close. Britain had urged its citizens to take advantage of the evacuation, saying no more attempts would be made to get people out.
The Nigerians agreed a city-wide ceasefire with the coup leaders on Monday night but said on Tuesday they were flying in reinforcements.
